text: Hello, this is Grete. Two questions have waited a long time: what was in the handkerchief, and what happened to the Rosens? In these last two chapters, Uncle Henrik finally explains, and the story reaches its end. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapters 16 and 17, and edit your essay. Today’s question: what can a novel tell you that a history book never could?

Today, read with two pencils in your mind. One marks the facts, the things a history book could tell you. The other marks the inside of the moment: what Annemarie notices, fears and hopes. At the end, say in one sentence what the story gave you that a list of facts couldn’t.

The model is a short sentence about Uncle Henrik explaining. The sentence to fix uses the same sound-alike word three times, and only one of them is right. One should point to a place, and one should show belonging. Read each in its spot and decide. Then add the marks that separate a list of three.

Today you stop hunting and start using. In grammar and spelling, you’ll study how a sentence gets fixed, and then choose the right sound-alike word yourself. Read each sentence for its meaning first. Ask what the word has to do in that spot, and the spelling will follow.

The street is getting brighter. Today two words take the shape root and two take a bending root. One of them is a word for clothes that make everyone match. Think about what is being shaped, or what is bending, and light four more windows.

Match these four words again, and this time try to do it in your head before you tap. Then look ahead. Two of these words, compare and conclude, are exactly what you’ll be doing with the Afterword in the next lesson.

First you watch an editor at work. Read the before sentence out loud. It sounds perfect, and it’s full of mistakes. That’s what makes these words so tricky. Then fill in each blank by asking what the word means there, and fix one last sentence on your own.

Same move, new sentences. Every answer comes from the word bank, and each one sounds just like two others. So say the meaning to yourself first: belonging, a place, they are, toward, very, or a number. Then pick the spelling that carries that meaning.

Today’s Courage Watch is about a whole town being brave together. After the war, I learned how many people on our street had helped: the baker, the woman upstairs, the boy who delivered the papers. None of them ever told anyone. Annemarie’s run was one run among hundreds. Listen to how Uncle Henrik talks about the others.

These are the last two chapters, so read them slowly. In Chapter 16, Uncle Henrik answers the questions Annemarie has been carrying, and his answer about the handkerchief is real history. Then Chapter 17 jumps ahead in time. Let it surprise you. Notice what is joyful and what is hard, and how Lowry lets both be true.

This is the very last sentence of the book. Look how small it is. Lowry doesn’t explain the war or tell you what Annemarie learned. She ends on one promise, and she puts the promise last, after the speaker. When you mimic it, end on a short promise, and let it have the final words.

Now you write. The questions ask what the handkerchief did, what Annemarie kept safe all this long time, and what your conclusion is about her courage. Then you’ll run an editing pass on your essay: sound-alike words, contractions, verbs that agree, and capital letters.

The last question asks for your conclusion about Annemarie. Think about the whole book, not just these chapters. Where did her courage start? How did it grow? And remember that real Danes did these things too. A strong conclusion looks back, and then it looks forward.

Last time you fixed how your essay sounds. Now you fix how it looks. Reading aloud won’t catch the wrong sound-alike word, so you have to look at each one. Check your contractions, check that each verb matches its subject, and check every capital letter. That’s editing.

On the day Denmark was free, my father took me into the city. Every shop seemed to be shut. On one door, someone had hung a sign: Closed because of joy. My father read it out loud and laughed until he cried. I have never forgotten that sign. Look at the two young men beside it. Even that day, they kept watch.
Transform. To change from one shape into another.
Uniform. One shape, so everyone matches.
Inflect. To bend your voice, to change how a word sounds.
Deflect. To bend something away. Twelve windows are lit.
